# FlightByte documentation

> Flight intelligence, byte by byte.

Base URL: https://api.flightbyte.dev/v1. Authentication: the `x-api-key` header.

---

# Introduction

> What FlightByte does, the two requests most integrations are made of, and where to go next.

Source: https://flightbyte.dev/docs

FlightByte is a flight status API built for the code on the receiving end. Look a flight up, or ask it to watch one.

## The shape of it

Everything lives under one base URL and one header.

```bash
# Look a flight up
curl "https://api.flightbyte.dev/v1/flights/TK/1848/2026-09-12" -H "x-api-key: $FLIGHTBYTE_KEY"
```

---

# Authentication and quotas

> The API key header, the quota windows on every key, and what a 429 looks like.

Source: https://flightbyte.dev/docs/authentication

## The key

Every request carries your key in the `x-api-key` header. `Authorization: Bearer <key>` is accepted too.

## Quotas

Your keys share three independent windows: requests per minute, per day and per month. Free has a cap of 3 watched flights; the fourth is refused with `402` and `watched_flight_limit`.

## When a window is full

The request is refused with `429`, a `Retry-After` header, and a body that names the window and `retryAfterSeconds`. Wait that long before retrying.

---

# Flights

> Looking flights up, choosing a leg when a number flies twice, the timeline, and how caching works.

Source: https://flightbyte.dev/docs/flights

## Looking a flight up

Address a flight by carrier, flight number and the local departure date at the origin.

## Leg selection

Flight numbers are not unique within a day. `TK1` operates two legs: SAW to AMS in the morning and IST to JFK in the afternoon. Pass `origin` to choose the leg; a subscription without a selector is refused with `400` and the list of `legs`.

## Caching

Lookups are served from cache while fresh; `refresh=true` skips it.

---

# Webhooks

> The delivery format, every event and change type, how to verify signatures, and what retries look like.

Source: https://flightbyte.dev/docs/webhooks

A webhook is a `POST` with a JSON body to your subscription's URL.

## Change types

Values for the `events` filter: `flight.departed`, `flight.arrived`, `departure.gate.changed`, `arrival.baggage.changed`.

## Verifying a delivery

The signature header is `t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>` where `v1` is HMAC-SHA256 of the timestamp and the raw body. Verify the signature against the raw bytes before parsing JSON.

```md
---

# Not a page: a SKILL.md example inside a code fence

## Not a section either
```

## Retries and suspension

Failed deliveries are retried up to 8 times with exponential backoff. Twenty consecutive failures suspend the subscription.

---

# Verifying webhook signatures the right way

> Raw body, timing-safe compare, replay window: the three ways signature verification goes wrong.

Source: https://flightbyte.dev/guides/verifying-webhook-signatures

A webhook is an unauthenticated POST from the internet. The signature is what makes it yours.

## Mistake one: verifying the wrong bytes

Frameworks parse JSON before your handler runs. Verify the signature against the raw body.

---

# Flight phase

> Where a flight is in its life, as one of ten values from scheduled to arrived.

Source: https://flightbyte.dev/glossary/flight-phase

The phase is derived from the airline status code and the times that exist: scheduled, boarding, departed, en_route, landed, arrived, cancelled, diverted, redirected, unknown.
